paragraphs.heading: Where land meets the deep sea
paragraphs.text: A continental margin is the outer rim of a continent's crust, the place where it butts up against oceanic crust beneath coastal seas. Geologists count it as one of three big zones of the seafloor, alongside the deep-ocean basins and the mid-ocean ridges. Margins take up roughly 28% of the ocean's area.

paragraphs.heading: The shelf
paragraphs.text: Every margin has three parts: the continental shelf, the continental slope and the continental rise. Nearest the shore is the shelf, a fairly shallow and generally flat stretch of seabed running out from the coast toward open ocean. Shelves are thought to make up 7% of the sea floor, and their width ranges from 0.03 to 1500 km. The shelf ends at the shelf break, where the seabed suddenly tilts far more steeply.

paragraphs.heading: Down the slope to the rise
paragraphs.text: Beyond the break lies the continental slope, which can stand 1–5 km above the deep-ocean floor. Submarine canyons often slice into it; they tend to be V-shaped, with nearly vertical walls, and they can carve all the way down to the abyssal plain. At the foot of the slope the angle drops sharply and the seabed begins to level out. That gentler zone is the continental rise, the outermost part of the margin.

paragraphs.heading: Active margins
paragraphs.text: Margins come in two kinds, active and passive. Active margins usually sit at plate boundaries and are busy places, with volcanoes and earthquakes. The west coasts of North and South America are examples, and such margins tend to be narrow out to the shelf break before plunging steeply into trenches. Most are convergent, where an oceanic plate meets a continental one and the denser oceanic crust sinks beneath the lighter continental crust.

paragraphs.heading: Transform and passive margins
paragraphs.text: A rarer active kind, the transform margin, forms where an oceanic plate and a continental plate slide past each other in opposite directions. Many faults offshore there build rugged relief of islands, shallow banks and deep basins, known as the continental borderland. Passive margins usually lie inside plates, far from their edges, with little tectonic activity, and they often face mid-ocean ridges. They are much wider and gentler than active margins, with low land running for miles back from the beach, long rivers, and piles of sediment building up on the shelf. The East Coast of the United States is one.

paragraphs.heading: Where river sediment ends up
paragraphs.text: As continental rock weathers and wears away, it breaks down mostly into sand and clay, and much of it washes into rivers that empty into the sea. Of all the sediment rivers carry, 80% gets trapped and spread across continental margins. Shelves also hold a lot of glacial and relict sediment, laid down when sea level was lower. Passive margins can store several kilometres of sediment, which helps scientists study how ocean basins first formed, while on active margins tectonic activity often destroys such deposits.

paragraphs.heading: Why the shelf is valuable
paragraphs.text: In money terms, no part of the ocean is worth more than the shelf. It is often also the most productive and most studied part of the margin, since its shallow water is easy to reach. The spread of offshore drilling and mining, and the limits of fisheries, led to a United Nations treaty on the law of the sea, known as UNCLOS. Under it, the edge of the margin is one test for how far a country's claim to undersea resources reaches. Those resources include fishing grounds, oil and gas, sand, gravel and some heavy minerals, and valuable metal ores are thought to occur along certain active margins.
